headline: Skip equal choices at the same recursion depth
statement: Given an integer array nums that may contain duplicate values, return every distinct full-length permutation in any order. Every input occurrence must be used exactly once in a permutation.
prerequisites: Basic Python lists, loops, and functions
intuition: Equal values are indistinguishable in the final word but still occupy separate input positions. Sort them, track used positions, and allow a later equal occurrence only after its predecessor has been used. That gives each value sequence one canonical assignment of positions.
approach: Sort nums and initialize used flags.
At each depth try unused positions.
Skip nums[i] when it equals the previous value and that previous position is unused.
Append, mark used, recurse, then undo both changes.
correctness: Every leaf uses every index exactly once and is a valid permutation. Among equal values the rule forces indices to be chosen in increasing order; therefore one value sequence has exactly one index assignment. Any distinct sequence can use that canonical assignment, so none are omitted.
bruteForce: Generate all n! index permutations and deduplicate full value lists. This wastes branches for repeated values.

complexity.explanation: There are at most n! leaves and copying each leaf costs n; duplicate pruning reduces the actual count.

pitfalls: The unused-predecessor rule prunes equivalent sibling branches immediately. Reversing the condition can still produce the correct complete permutations, but explores many prefixes that cannot be completed.
Undo both the path and used flag.
A set of used values would wrongly remove repeated occurrences.
